title: Serving runtime resilience field guide and operator playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:

This field guide consolidates operator-facing runbook actions, calibration guidance for chaos and resilience tests, and deterministic fallback recipes for common partial-failure modes in the Redwood serving runtime. It is written for SREs and runtime engineers who must keep inference SLOs during hardware flakiness, kernel regressions, and network partitions.

Goals:
- Restore or preserve 95th/99th latency SLOs or provide acceptable graceful-degradation behavior within 10 minutes for production incidents.
- Validate that fallback chains (model variants, quantized fallbacks, regional draining) trigger with predictable, auditable steps.
- Provide reproducible chaos calibration recipes so experiments are safe and informative.

Who should use this doc:
- Oncall SREs executing incident playbooks.
- Platform engineers validating rollout gates and kernel rollbacks.
- Release engineers preparing canary plans for scheduling/kernel changes.

Key runbook sections (quick links):
1) Triage heuristics and immediate mitigation (p.1)
2) Deterministic fallback invocation recipes (p.4)
3) Hardware/network partial-failure drills (p.7)
4) Chaos calibration lab guide (p.11)
5) Post-incident follow-ups and RCA template (p.15)

1) Triage heuristics and immediate mitigation

Symptoms -> quick checks (first 5 minutes):
- Elevated 95th/99th tail latency
  - Check per-kernel P95/P99 in runtime-kernel telemetry dashboard (panel: kernel-latency-by-workload).
  - Query: `SELECT kernel, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms FROM runtime_latency WHERE window=5m`
- Increased retry counts or gRPC stream resets
  - Check connection reset rate across dispatcher nodes and frontends.
- Drop in throughput with stable input traffic
  - Check GPU utilization, and kernel queue length on the affected pool.

Immediate mitigations (order matters):
1. Short-term routing: shift traffic off the suspected pool regionally using the routing control API. Command: `redwoodctl routing weight --pool <pool-id> --set 0.0 --reason "emergency-drain"`
2. Enable conservative admission controller: flip the admission gate to `slo-conservative` for affected service. CLI: `redwoodctl admission set --service <svc> --profile slo-conservative`
3. Activate model-variant fallback for critical endpoints only (see section 2). Use `--scope` to avoid global behavioral changes.
4. If kernel-specific traces exist (trace-id), collect live kernel trace bundles and attach to the incident ticket: `redwood-trace collect --trace-id <id> --output /tmp/trace.tgz`

2) Deterministic fallback invocation recipes

Fallback types supported (and recommended use-cases):
- Model-variant fallback: swap to a smaller model shard or lower-fidelity quantized variant to preserve latency for critical endpoints. Use when latency spikes but correctness can be marginally reduced.
- Local KV-prefetch bypass: disable speculative KV prefetch on the pool to reduce queuing in cold paths. Use when kernel stalls are queue-related.
- Regional reroute: move traffic to a healthy region replica when a hardware domain (rack/NVLink island) is implicated. Use when interconnect errors appear in telemetry.

Activation steps: Model-variant fallback (safe scoped):
1. Identify endpoint route(s) affected: `redwoodctl route list --filter "p95>200ms"`
2. Create a scoped policy:
```
redwoodctl policy create --name "emergency-variant-fallback-<incident-id>" \  --scope routes=<route-id1>,<route-id2> \  --action model_variant --variant smaller-llm-q4_1 --ttl 30m
```
3. Verify traffic is handled by checking `model_variant_switch{policy="emergency-variant-fallback-<incident-id>"}` in metrics within 2 minutes.
4. Escalate to runtime owners if P95 does not improve within 10 minutes.

Rollback steps:
- Revoke the policy: `redwoodctl policy delete --name <policy>`
- Confirm traffic returns to baseline model by checking the model catalog assignment (`redwoodctl model assign --route <route-id> --catalog-entry <id>`) and validating end-to-end latency.

3) Hardware/network partial-failure drills

Common failure patterns and operator steps:
A) NVLink flap / interconnect errors (symptoms: kernel retries, partial model swap churn)
- Quick checks: `nvidia-smi topo --matrix` (on node), `dmesg` for PCIe/NVLink errors, runtime telemetry `nvlink_error_count`
- Mitigation: reduce batch concurrency on affected nodes (`redwoodctl node set --node <id> --batch-concurrency 1`) and move traffic away from the node pool. Consider a controlled rolling reboot if hardware vendor recommends it.

B) GPU thermal-induced throttling (symptoms: sustained throughput drop + GPU freq drop)
- Check GPU telemetry: `gpu_temperature_celsius`, `gpu_power_draw_watts`, `gpu_clocks_mhz`
- Mitigation: mark node `cordon` and route collector jobs away, allow graceful termination of in-flight requests, then perform cooling window and manual hardware inspection.

C) Rack-level network partition (symptoms: partial dispatcher connectivity, cross-rack p95 increases)
- Use `redwoodctl network diag --rack <rack-id>` to collect connectivity graphs.
- Mitigation: enable cross-region fallback policy and set `max_inflight_per_route` lower to avoid head-of-line blocking.

4) Chaos calibration lab guide (safe, repeatable experiments)

Purpose: calibrate the amount and kind of fault injection to surface realistic resilience gaps without producing noisy or unsafe outages. All experiments must run in a dedicated staging fleet.

Principles:
- Start small and increment: inject low-frequency faults and step up based on verified metrics.
- Use traffic shadowing for realistic request shapes.
- Always have an abort button (policy to immediately revert routing/admission) and a telemetry watch (automated alert that halts the experiment).

Sample calibration protocol: NVLink stress calibration
1. Environment: staging pool with representative models and request trace replay (shadow traffic).
2. Baseline: run replay for 30 minutes, capture p50/p95/p99, kernel retries, and throughput.
3. Inject: use the chaos harness to flip a virtual NVLink error rate on target nodes at 0.1% of packets for 10 minutes. YAML snippet for the harness:
```
chaos_test:
  name: nvlink-perturbation-calibration
  targets:
    - node_selector: pool=staging-gpu
  injection:
    type: nvlink_error_rate
    rate: 0.001
    duration: 600s
  abort_on:
    - metric: runtime.p99_latency
      threshold: 1.5x_baseline
```
4. Observe: If P99 > 1.5x baseline or kernel retry rate > 10x baseline, stop the injection and capture traces.
5. Increment: increase rate to 0.5% only if safety thresholds are not breached.

Measuring experiment value:
- Record the minimal injection rate that produces consistent P99 degradation — this is the fleet fragility index for NVLink. Track over time.

5) Post-incident follow-ups and RCA template

Minimum deliverables after any production intervention:
- Incident timeline (wall-clocked) with actions and actor names.
- Telemetry extracts: pre-incident, incident window, and 2x recovery period.
- Minimal actionable root cause (hardware/kernel/operator) and one prioritized remediation (short, medium, long-term).
- Test plan to validate the remediation in staging (include chaos calibration adjustments).

RCA template (copy/paste):
- Title: Short sentence summarizing outage
- Impact: SLOs breached, customer visible impact, duration
- Timeline: bulletized timeline with timestamps and actions
- Root cause analysis: primary cause and supporting evidence (logs, traces, kernel dumps)
- Mitigations: what we did during the incident and why it helped
- Fixes: short/medium/long term with owners and ETA
- Postmortem checklist items: capacity, monitoring, runbook updates, PRs created

Operational tooling and queries (cheat sheet)
- See current admission profile: `redwoodctl admission get --service <svc>`
- Force a model-variant switch for a route (scoped): `redwoodctl policy create --name emergency-switch --scope routes=<route> --action model_variant --variant <id>`
- Collect kernel trace: `redwood-trace collect --trace-id <id> --query 'kernel:*' --output /tmp/kernel-trace.tgz`
- Cordon node from scheduler: `redwoodctl node cordon --node <id> --reason "investigation"`

Ownership and escalation
- First responder: Oncall SRE (runtime-sre rotation) — execute triage and immediate mitigations.
- Secondary: Runtime kernel lead — investigate kernel traces and decide on kernel rollback.
- Tertiary: Platform owner — approve regional failover and cross-region policy changes.
- Pager escalation matrix: follow the team directory in People Ops; aim to escalate to kernel lead within 20 minutes if mitigations fail.

Safety and governance
- All production policy changes triggered by this runbook must be backed by an incident ticket and remain auditable.
- Chaos experiments must be registered in the experiment registry with a runbook link, expected metrics and abort conditions.

Appendix A — Example dashboard panels to check
- kernel-latency-by-workload: stacked p50/p95/p99 per kernel
- nvlink_error_count: NVLink errors per node, 1m/5m windows
- model_variant_switch: counts and policy labels
- admission_profile_effectiveness: admitted vs rejected requests per profile

Appendix B — Quick glossary
- Kernel: execution unit (e.g., attention-shard, kv-prefetch, softmax-quant) scheduled on GPU.
- Admission controller: runtime component that shapes inbound requests by policy profiled to SLOs.
- Model-variant: a functionally similar served artifact with different fidelity/cost characteristics.
